metaDescription: Gross lease vs net lease explained simply for Newcastle businesses. Learn what goes into each lease type, what costs you'll actually pay, and what to watch for before signing.
excerpt: Most tenants in Newcastle don't know the difference between a gross lease and a net lease until they get the first outgoings bill. This guide breaks it down properly.

body:
## What is a Gross Lease?

In a gross lease, you pay one fixed rent amount per month. The landlord covers outgoings — rates, taxes, insurance, maintenance, the lot.

Your headline rent is your headline rent. Simple.

**Common in:** Single-tenanted buildings, smaller Newcastle commercial suites, older fit-for-purpose offices.

**The trap:** Outgoings can be built into the headline rent, so you're paying them anyway — just invisibly. And when costs rise, some landlords use a gross lease structure to absorb increases quietly.

---

## What is a Net Lease?

In a net lease, you pay base rent *plus* your share of the building's outgoings.

There are three main levels:

### Net Lease (Single Net)

You pay rent plus your proportion of council rates only. Landlords handle everything else.

**Rare in Newcastle.** Usually seen in multi-tenanted strata buildings.

### Double Net Lease (NN)

You pay rent plus your share of council rates and building insurance. Structural maintenance is the landlord's problem.

**More common in Newcastle.** Common in industrial estates and multi-unit commercial centres.

### Triple Net Lease (NNN)

You pay rent plus council rates, building insurance, and all maintenance costs.

**Most common in commercial investment property.** You'll be responsible for repairs, refurbishment, roof, carpark, everything.

Landlords love NNN leases because their income is clean. Tenants often underestimate how much maintenance actually costs.

---

## Gross vs Net: The Key Differences

| | Gross Lease | Net Lease (NN/NNN) |
|---|---|---|
| Rent | Fixed headline rent | Base rent + outgoings |
| Predictability | Higher | Lower |
| Risk | Landlord carries outgoings risk | You carry outgoings risk |
| Transparency | Often opaque | More transparent |
| Common for | Smaller suites, older buildings | Investment-grade properties |

---

## What Goes Into Outgoings?

In a Newcastle NNN or double net lease, outgoings typically include:

- **Council rates** — based on the property's assessed value
- **Land tax** — if the landlord hasn't opted out
- **Building insurance** — full replacement value
- **Maintenance and repairs** — including reactive and planned maintenance
- **Body corporate / strata levies** — if applicable
- **Cleaning and landscaping** — common area upkeep
- **Plant and equipment servicing** — lifts, HVAC, fire systems

Outgoings in Newcastle currently range from **$80–$180/sqm/year** depending on the building, age, and services provided.

Get the actual outgoings figure from the landlord in writing before you sign anything.

---

## What to Look at When Reviewing a Property

These are the things that cost tenants the most money in a net lease. Get inside every space you're considering.

### Roof

In a NNN lease, the roof is your problem. Ask how old it is, when it was last inspected, and whether there's a current maintenance schedule. A 20-year-old metal roof with patch repair history will eventually need a full replacement — and that bill lands with you. If there's any doubt about condition, get a building inspector to assess it before you sign.

### Mechanical Systems (Air Conditioning)

Ask when the HVAC system was last serviced, how old the units are, and whether there's a current maintenance contract in place. In older Newcastle commercial buildings, air conditioning units from the early 2000s are still running. They work — until they don't. A failed air conditioning unit in a office tenancy can cost $8,000–$20,000 to replace, and that comes out of your budget, not the landlord's.

### Car Spaces

Find out exactly how many car spaces are included in the lease and what the arrangement is for any additional spaces. Landlords will often advertise a space with generous car space inclusion but bury the fact that only two spaces are included and the rest cost extra — sometimes $150–$250 per space per month on top of base rent. Make sure the car space arrangement matches your team's actual needs before you lock in.

---

## Other Things to Consider When Looking at Spaces

### Get the outgoings figure upfront

Don't sign a lease without knowing exactly what outgoings you'll be paying on top of base rent. Ask for two years of outgoings history. If they can't provide it, walk away.

### Understand the fitout contribution

In a net lease, you're inheriting whatever condition the previous tenant left the space in. If the air conditioning is 15 years old and the roof is leaking, that's your problem. Budget for a fitout allowance in your lease negotiation or push for a rent-free period to cover it.

### Negotiate rent reviews carefully

Most net leases have fixed annual increases or CPI reviews. But in a rising market, a landlord will push for market rent reviews on top of that. Make sure your lease caps review mechanisms and defines what "market rent" actually means.

### Factor in make-good obligations

Most commercial leases require you to hand the space back in the same condition you received it — or better. Factor in the cost of dismantle, removal, and making good when you're budgeting your lease exit costs.

### Know the landlord's track record

A good landlord in a NNN lease stays out of your way and responds to maintenance requests quickly. A bad one charges you for everything and delays repairs until the building deteriorates. Talk to current or former tenants in the building before you sign.

---

## The Bottom Line

A gross lease is not automatically better. A net lease is not automatically worse.

What matters is:

1. **What the actual total cost is** — not just the headline rent
2. **What you're responsible for** — and what you can realistically afford
3. **Whether the building is being maintained** — because in a net lease, the maintenance standard is your problem

A good tenant representative will walk you through the lease structure, flag what you don't see in the advertised rent, and negotiate terms that actually work for your business — not just the landlord's.
